source_artifacts.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)

inputs.source: supplier portal upload (invoice document authored by an external supplier)

instructions.note: The agent is instructed to update vendor bank details directly from unauthenticated invoice content ('If the invoice shows new bank details, update the vendor record'), with no independent, out-of-band verification step required before acting.

The sole control against bank-detail and payment fraud is a model-authored one-line summary reviewed by a clerk. No structural control (destination confirmation, full-detail display, change-history flag) backs the instruction.

controls.name: Clerk approval card before payment or bank change
controls.decay_rationale: The gate itself lives outside the model, but the approver only sees a model-authored one-line summary, not raw bank account numbers or change history (runtime notes). A more persuasive model can write incomplete or misleading summaries (ASI09), and approval fatigue at roughly 150 cards/day further reduces per-card scrutiny (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Out-of-band destination confirmation for bank detail changes
controls.decay_rationale: A control that verifies new bank details via a channel not derived from the invoice (e.g., a callback to the vendor's on-file phone number) is bound to the system of record, not to model output, so it does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Least-privilege ERP credential scoping
controls.decay_rationale: Scoping the credential (per-vendor or per-amount limits) would not decay with model capability and would shrink blast radius even if bank_update is fraudulently triggered.

controls.name: Raw-action approval review showing account numbers and change history
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the approver the actual destination account, prior value, and recency of change (rather than a model summary) removes the model as the sole interpreter of the action, independent of model capability.

findings.title: Summary-gated irreversible action (TC9): invoice-injected bank detail change approved without raw evidence

attack_path.note: Untrusted supplier invoice content claims new bank details
Agent reads current vendor master to match invoice/PO
Agent updates vendor bank details based solely on the invoice's claim
Approval card shows only a one-line summary; account number and change history are not shown

forecast.watch_signal: The platform model is upgraded with no separate review (runtime notes). Watch for approval-card summaries that stay terse/confident even as the underlying model changes, and for any rise in approved cards per reviewer per day beyond the current ~150/day baseline.

evidence.observation: Instruction directs updating vendor bank details whenever 'the invoice shows new bank details,' with no independent verification step required before acting.
The only pre-action control described is a model-generated one-line summary reviewed by the clerk before any payment or bank change.

evidence.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)
evidence.observation: Card displays only vendor name, amount, and invoice/PO match; bank account number and prior bank details or change history are not shown to the approver.
Confirms: 'The card shows only the model's summary. Bank account numbers and the change history are not shown.'
'The ERP credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment' — a broad, non-least-privilege credential scope.

recommendations.action: Add a destination confirmation control that verifies any new bank details via an out-of-band channel (e.g., a callback to the vendor's on-file phone number, not contact info present in the invoice) before the vendor record is updated, independent of model output.
Change the approval card to raw_action review mode: show the actual bank account number (old vs. new) and change history rather than a model-authored summary.
Scope the ERP credential to least privilege (e.g., per-vendor or per-amount limits) instead of a single credential that can update any vendor and schedule any payment.

findings.title: Summary-gated irreversible action (TC9): payment scheduled to a possibly fraudulent account with no visibility into a recent bank change

attack_path.note: Vendor bank details changed based on the invoice's claim (see finding f1-bank-detail-redirect-via-invoice)
Agent schedules payment to the vendor's current, possibly just-redirected, bank account
Second approval card shows amount/vendor/invoice match only; does not flag that bank details changed recently

forecast.watch_signal: Model/platform upgrades ship without separate review (runtime notes). Watch for approval summaries that continue to omit bank-change context while daily volume (~150 cards/day) holds or rises, compounding approval fatigue with a more persuasive model.

evidence.observation: 'Schedule payment on the due date' runs immediately after any bank-detail update, with no explicit requirement to cross-check for recent bank changes in the payment approval summary.

evidence.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)
evidence.observation: Card shows amount, vendor, and invoice/PO match only — no mention of the vendor's bank details having changed.
Clerk approves roughly 150 cards per day, consistent with approval fatigue reducing per-card scrutiny (SAFE-T1403).

'The ERP credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment' — the same broad credential performs both the write and the spend, so the agent that made the fraudulent change is also the one authorized to pay against it.

recommendations.action: Require the payment approval summary to explicitly flag when the destination bank details were changed within N days of the payment being scheduled, sourced from the system of record rather than model narration.
Add anomaly detection and a mandatory cooling-off period between a bank-detail change and the first payment to that account.

rating.rationale: An untrusted supplier invoice can directly trigger two S3 (severe) sinks — an ERP vendor bank-detail configure and a payment spend — using a broad, non-least-privilege credential. Inherent risk is critical for both paths (U source to S3 sink). The only control is a human approval gate, which is structural but classified partially_dependent because approval_review_mode is model_summary: the clerk sees a one-line, model-authored summary and neither the raw bank account number nor the change history. Per rubric section 5 step 2, this caps the credit at -2 tiers with a floor of moderate, giving residual risk of moderate for both findings. No structural control severs either path (no destination confirmation bound to the system of record, no least-privilege credential scoping), so these are the highest-priority gaps. The forecast is driven by the model_upgrade trigger: runtime notes state the model is upgraded with the platform and no separate review, which is exactly the trigger that defeats a model_summary approval gate (control_decay.md), and is compounded by approval fatigue at roughly 150 cards/day. Once ctl.clerk_approval's credit is removed, both findings return to critical. The single highest-leverage fix is converting the approval gate to raw_action review and adding an out-of-band destination confirmation bound to the vendor record rather than to invoice content.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration artifacts (system prompt, the rendered approval card, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior or a live penetration test.

No ERP tool manifest, IaC, or credential policy document was provided; credential scope ('broad', can update any vendor and schedule any payment) and the classification of bank-detail update as a 'configure' action are inferred from runtime notes and the system prompt, at medium confidence.
No MCP configuration or agent card was provided for the ERP integration; if additional protocol-level controls or vulnerabilities exist, they were not assessed.
Autonomy step and runtime limits (max_unattended_steps, max_runtime_minutes) are not specified in any artifact and were treated as null/unbounded per the rubric's autonomy modifier rule.
